items.streamTitle: BIABench expanded bias testing from static answers to interactive behavior
items.streamSummary: BIABench is a preprint benchmark designed to assess bias in interactive AI systems across multi-turn tasks rather than only isolated prompts. Reported results show that disparities can emerge through trajectories even when single responses appear acceptable. The benchmark does not by itself measure real-world harm, but it provides a stronger testing unit for agents that take sequential actions.

items.streamTitle: StateGuard targeted corruption of long-running agent state
items.streamSummary: StateGuard is a preprint approach for protecting persistent agent state during multi-step workflows. The reported tests reduced some state-corruption failures by checking transitions and maintaining stronger state controls. The results are benchmark-specific, but the architecture reinforces a broader security principle: long-running agents need protection for internal state as well as input filters.

items.streamTitle: Theory-of-Planned-Behavior variables predicted cyber-harassment intentions in a cross-sectional model
items.streamSummary: A Saudi survey modeled cyber-harassment intentions using attitudes, perceived norms, and perceived behavioral control. Several planned-behavior constructs were associated with intentions, but all variables were measured in the same cross-sectional survey. The study is useful for hypothesis structure, not proof that changing a modeled mediator will reduce actual harassment.

items.streamTitle: NATO's top commander said hybrid attacks aim to break allied will, while urging public attribution
items.streamSummary: NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich urged governments to attribute sabotage, cyberattacks, and drone activity that he said were intended to weaken support for Ukraine. The statement is an important strategic assessment, not proof that every cited incident was Russian-directed or that the campaign has changed allied behavior. It illustrates the need to separate event, attribution, intent, and effect.

items.streamTitle: A quantitative FRAM model mapped 98 functions in surgical scheduling and surfaced candidate bottlenecks
items.streamSummary: Researchers applied FRAM and FRAMalyse to a hospital surgical-scheduling process, using interviews and observations to model 98 interconnected functions. The analysis highlighted high-variability and high-coupling activities that could become bottlenecks. The model is a structured representation of sociotechnical work, not proof that changing the highest-ranked function will improve scheduling. Operational validation is the next step.
items.attribution: Rashid et al. — International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery

items.streamTitle: Russian strikes expanded to Ukrainian telecom and data infrastructure
items.streamSummary: Reuters reported Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunications and data infrastructure, including Kyivstar facilities and data centers. Operators and officials described service disruptions affecting communications. The attacks show that digital infrastructure is part of wartime resilience, but physical damage and mission impact are not the same outcome. Recovery time, redundancy, and continuity should be tracked separately.

items.streamTitle: Digital literacy was strongly associated with AI-chatbot adoption among football coaches
items.streamSummary: An international survey of 213 professional football coaches found that digital literacy was strongly associated with AI-chatbot adoption and statistically accounted for several age- and experience-related differences. The study identified a useful competency threshold in its sample, but the cross-sectional mediation cannot prove that improving digital literacy will cause adoption. A training intervention would be the stronger next test.

items.streamTitle: Temporal motifs changed which nodes appeared important in dynamic networks
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study incorporated recurring temporal motifs into node ranking and found that dynamic interaction patterns can identify importance differently from static network measures. The method is useful when sequence and timing matter, but high rank still does not establish causal leverage, feasibility, or intervention value. Those require separate evidence.

items.streamTitle: Vectorized simulation accelerated reinforcement learning for microrobot control
items.streamSummary: A machine-learning study used vectorized simulation to train microrobot control policies at much higher throughput. The reported policies performed well in the simulated tasks, showing how parallel environments can reduce training cost. The evidence does not eliminate sim-to-real uncertainty: physical noise, sensing, and actuation can change performance when policies leave the simulator.

items.streamTitle: EvoPathBench tested whether agents can update reasoning as pathways change
items.streamSummary: EvoPathBench is a preprint benchmark for agent reasoning over evolving multi-step pathways. It is designed to expose systems that rely on static retrieval or memorized patterns when intermediate relationships change. Reported results show meaningful performance variation across agents. The benchmark is useful for adaptation testing, but success on synthetic tasks does not itself establish reliable reasoning in real operational systems.

items.streamTitle: Co-speech gestures were coupled with whole-body postural dynamics
items.streamSummary: A laboratory study measured gestures and postural sway during speech and found coordinated changes between the two. The result suggests that visible communicative movement is embedded in a wider motor system rather than being an isolated channel. It does not establish a psychological meaning for any one posture signal, but it cautions against treating body-language features as independent indicators.

items.streamTitle: Changing training emphasis altered selective-attention gains in older adults
items.streamSummary: An experiment with older adults found that what participants were instructed to emphasize during attention training changed the pattern of improvement. Benefits were selective rather than evidence of a general cognitive boost. The result is relevant to training design because task instructions can become part of the intervention; transfer beyond the practiced task still needs separate evidence.

items.streamTitle: Founder identity changed how prior failure affected funding judgments
items.streamSummary: A conjoint experiment examined how investors evaluate founders after prior venture failure. Results indicated that Latinx identity interacted with failure-related judgments under some conditions rather than producing one constant penalty. The study concerns stated investment choices in an experimental design, not observed capital flows, but it shows why bias can emerge through interactions between identity and performance history.

items.streamTitle: U.S. and Indian forces integrated drones, air assault, and live fire at Yudh Abhyas 2026
items.streamSummary: The U.S. Army reported that Yudh Abhyas 2026 integrated American and Indian formations across command-post work, air assault, drones, weapons exchange, and combined live fire. The exercise demonstrates practical interoperability activity rather than a measured change in combat effectiveness. Useful follow-on metrics include communications reliability, cross-unit handoffs, target processing, and performance under degraded conditions.

items.streamTitle: A U.S. appeals court upheld the Pentagon's supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic
items.streamSummary: A U.S. appeals court upheld the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a national-security supply-chain risk, a decision with significant procurement and reputational consequences. The dispute centered partly on Anthropic's restrictions on certain military uses. The ruling resolves a legal stage, not the underlying technical question of whether the company's safeguards create operational risk or improve safety.

items.streamTitle: Social-media detox evidence was mixed rather than uniformly beneficial
items.streamSummary: A review of social-media detox interventions found mixed effects across wellbeing outcomes and designs. Some studies reported benefits, while others found small or null changes. The evidence does not support treating a temporary break as a universal solution to digital harms. Effects depend on the outcome, intervention, and population being measured.

items.streamTitle: Agent trace deletion reduced context burden but created state-loss risk
items.streamSummary: A preprint tested ways for long-running agents to delete or compress parts of their execution history. Selective removal can reduce context cost, but the same mechanism can discard information later needed for debugging, recovery, or verification. The work reinforces that memory optimization is a governance problem as well as a performance problem: provenance and recoverability need explicit protection.

items.streamTitle: Perceived political coalitions shaped judgments beyond simple ideology
items.streamSummary: Experiments showed that people organize political actors into perceived coalitions and use those relational structures when making judgments. The finding suggests that political cognition is not reducible to one-dimensional ideology: who is seen as allied with whom can change interpretation. The studies are controlled experiments, so the size and durability of these effects in live political environments remain separate questions.

items.streamTitle: An MCP agent-to-agent attack showed how malicious instructions can cross tool boundaries
items.streamSummary: A preprint demonstrated an agent-to-agent attack in Model Context Protocol workflows, showing how malicious content introduced in one component can influence downstream tools or agents. The result is configuration-dependent, not evidence that every MCP deployment is vulnerable. Its broader value is architectural: trust boundaries, provenance, and action authorization need to persist across the whole connected workflow.

items.streamTitle: Visual-reasoning performance varied sharply across task types
items.streamSummary: A broad analysis of visual-reasoning systems found substantial variation across task families and representations. Aggregate performance therefore hid important weaknesses that emerged only on particular reasoning demands. The practical lesson is to test the visual operations a system actually needs to perform, rather than using a single benchmark average as evidence of general visual intelligence.

items.streamTitle: Wrong AI advice reduced people's willingness to say 'I don't know'
items.streamSummary: A controlled preprint found that confident but incorrect AI advice could reduce people's use of an 'I don't know' option and pull responses toward the model. The result matters because an assistant can alter confidence behavior even when it does not improve knowledge. The evidence comes from bounded tasks rather than consequential field decisions, so transfer to professional settings needs testing.

items.streamTitle: Serious-game co-creation improved design fit but did not by itself prove behavioral impact
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study described a stakeholder co-creation process for a serious game, showing how iterative participation can surface usability and implementation needs that designers might otherwise miss. The work supports co-creation as a development method, not as evidence that a co-created game automatically changes behavior. Outcome testing remains a separate stage.

items.streamTitle: Micro-randomized intervention data supported adaptive machine-learning decisions without abandoning experimentation
items.streamSummary: A study combined micro-randomized intervention opportunities with machine-learning decision rules, preserving randomized variation while exploring more personalized treatment timing. The approach is useful because it separates prediction from causal learning better than purely observational personalization. Results remain specific to the tested setting, and deployment still requires calibration and monitoring.

items.streamTitle: UK firms gained access to Ukraine's Avengers Labs data for AI drone-swarm development
items.streamSummary: The UK launched a competition allowing selected companies to use Ukraine's Avengers Labs battlefield datasets to develop AI-enabled drone swarms and collaborative autonomy. The initiative creates a concrete data-sharing and testing pathway between wartime experience and allied industry. It does not yet show that the resulting models improve swarm performance or survive contested conditions; those outcomes require later testing.
